issues.detail: Example 2 describes the rule and workflow in prose without showing the actual rule file, command output, or resulting diff, and Example 1 only sketches the agent's response, so the examples are less concrete than the rest of the skill.

scenarios.name: ci-sarif-no-account
scenarios.rationale: A uses all the rubric's flags exactly (`--sarif --output=semgrep.sarif`, `--baseline-commit=origin/${{ github.base_ref }}`, `--error`, fetch-depth 0, no token). B has the same structure but uses `--sarif-output`, which isn't the rubric's `--output` form. B also computes a merge-base instead of `origin/${{ github.base_ref }}`, so it misses the specified baseline form. B adds extras that don't offset those misses.

scenarios.name: custom-rule-hardcoded-key-and-missing-auth
scenarios.rationale: Both use patterns with metavariable-regex for the Stripe rule and give the validate and test commands with ruleid/ok annotations. B's auth rule is more thorough, with pattern-not variants for authMiddleware, but it relies on `pattern: $ROUTER.$METHOD("$PATH", ...)` plus regex filters. A's auth rule is closer to the rubric's literal shape (a pattern for the handler plus a pattern-not containing authMiddleware) but is narrow, matching only async arrow handlers on `router`. A also gets the Stripe rule's declaration forms less complete than B, which covers const, let, var and member assignment.

scenarios.name: private-code-offline-scan-and-autofix
scenarios.rationale: Both use --config .semgrep/ --metrics=off, -a/--autofix, and tell the user to review the diff because the fix is a text substitution; A explicitly warns that --config auto sends the project URL to the Registry and enables metrics, as the rubric asks, while B only says auto/p/ configs fetch rules and never mentions the project URL, but B's dryrun preview, fix tests, and safety caveats are stronger.
